name: Samuel anointing Saul (and later David)
scope: The old prophet Samuel makes -- and then unmakes -- Israel's first king, and finds the second in a shepherd boy no one thought to invite. T1: OPENING SCENE -- the people of Israel come to Samuel and demand a king 'like all the nations'; God tells Samuel to warn them what a king will take (their sons for chariots, their daughters for perfumers, a tenth of their harvest) but to give them one anyway (1 Samuel 8). T2: Saul, a tall young Benjaminite out looking for his father Kish's lost donkeys, stumbles onto Samuel; Samuel pours a flask of olive oil over Saul's head and kisses him, the private anointing (1 Samuel 9-10). T3: Saul is chosen publicly by lot at Mizpah and hides among the baggage; when they drag him out he stands 'head and shoulders above' everyone else (1 Samuel 10:22-23). T4: Saul disobeys about the Amalekite spoils -- 'to obey is better than sacrifice' (1 Samuel 15:22) -- and Samuel tears his robe and says the kingdom is torn from him; Samuel goes to Bethlehem, to Jesse's house, and passes over seven older sons ('the LORD looketh on the heart', 1 Samuel 16:7). T5: the youngest, David, is called in from the sheep -- 'ruddy, and withal of a beautiful countenance' -- and Samuel anoints him with the horn of oil while his brothers watch (1 Samuel 16:11-13). Further rungs: the Witch of Endor at 1 Samuel 28, where Saul makes the medium raise Samuel's ghost the night before Gilboa; Samuel's mother Hannah's prayer at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1-2) as the T1 anchor for who Samuel IS; the phrase 'Is Saul also among the prophets?' (1 Samuel 10:11).

DISTRACTOR MINE = adjacent real OT figures/objects/quotes (Eli at Shiloh; Elisha's mantle instead of Samuel's oil; 'Here am I, send me' from Isaiah instead of 'Speak, LORD, for thy servant heareth' from Samuel; Jonathan, Abner, Ish-bosheth as wrong-Saul-adjacent kings). history_overlap: The history bank owns the archaeology and dating of the united Israelite monarchy (~1000 BC, the Tel Dan stele's 'House of David' inscription, the debate over the scale of the kingdom); theology owns the STORY beats -- Kish's donkeys, the flask of oil, the baggage, the seven brothers, the horn.

name: David and Goliath
scope: The shepherd boy who dropped a giant with a stone from a brook. T1: OPENING SCENE -- the Philistine army camps on one hill, Israel's on another, the Valley of Elah between them; every morning Goliath of Gath, ~9 feet tall in a bronze helmet and a coat of mail 'five thousand shekels of brass' (1 Samuel 17:5), steps out and challenges any Israelite to single combat, and for forty days no one goes. T2: David, sent by his father Jesse with parched corn and ten cheeses to check on his older brothers, hears the challenge and volunteers; King Saul offers his own armour, but David can't walk in it and takes it off. T3: David goes down to the brook and picks up FIVE smooth stones and puts them in his shepherd's bag; he faces Goliath with a sling and a staff, and Goliath scorns him -- 'Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves?' (17:43). T4: David answers: 'Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts... this day will the LORD deliver thee into mine hand... that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel' (17:45-46). T5: David slings ONE stone, sinks it into Goliath's forehead, and the giant falls on his face; David runs, stands on Goliath, and cuts off his head with Goliath's own sword (17:49-51). Further rungs: Goliath's spear-shaft 'like a weaver's beam' (17:7); David later brings Goliath's head to Jerusalem and keeps his sword at the tabernacle at Nob, and asks for it back before fleeing Saul (1 Samuel 21:9); the Elhanan-vs-Goliath variant at 2 Samuel 21:19 (a real textual puzzle -- name it as such at T5 depth, not a contradiction to hide).

name: David and Jonathan (the sworn brotherhood + 'How are the mighty fallen')
scope: The oath-bound friendship of the king's son and the shepherd-king-to-be, and its ruin at Mount Gilboa. T1: OPENING SCENE -- after the Goliath fight Jonathan, King Saul's crown-prince son, meets David: 'the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David... and Jonathan loved him as his own soul' (1 Samuel 18:1); Jonathan strips off his own royal robe, sword, bow, and belt and gives them to David. T2: Saul, jealous, hurls a spear at David during a harp performance; Jonathan tests his father with a scheme at the new-moon feast and warns David with three arrows shot past a boy servant -- 'Is not the arrow beyond thee?' is the signal to flee (1 Samuel 20:37). T3: they meet secretly in a field, embrace and weep, and Jonathan makes David swear to spare his descendants; Jonathan says 'The LORD be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever' (20:42). T4: Jonathan dies with his father Saul and brothers on Mount Gilboa when the Philistines break the Israelite line; Saul, wounded, falls on his own sword rather than be captured; their bodies are pinned to the wall of Beth-shan and the men of Jabesh-gilead recover them by night and burn them under a tamarisk tree (1 Samuel 31). T5: David hears the news and composes 'the Song of the Bow', a lament taught to all Judah: 'The beauty of Israel is slain upon thy high places: how are the mighty fallen!' -- 'Ye mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew, neither let there be rain, upon you' -- 'thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women' (2 Samuel 1:19-27). Further rungs: David later finds Jonathan's crippled son Mephibosheth -- lame from being dropped as a five-year-old by his nurse when the news came -- and seats him at the king's own table (2 Samuel 4:4; 9:7-13).

name: David and Bathsheba and Nathan the prophet ('Thou art the man')
scope: Israel's greatest king sees a woman on a rooftop, sends her husband to die, and is broken by a prophet's parable. T1: OPENING SCENE -- 'at the time when kings go forth to battle' David stays home in Jerusalem while his general Joab besieges Rabbah of the Ammonites; walking on the palace roof at evening he sees Bathsheba bathing (2 Samuel 11:1-2). T2: David sends for her; she is 'the wife of Uriah the Hittite' -- one of David's own thirty mighty men. T3: when she is pregnant David recalls Uriah from the front and tries to make him sleep with her to cover it; Uriah refuses to go home while the ark and the army are in tents in the field, so David sends him back with a letter to Joab: 'Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die' (11:15). T4: after Uriah is killed, God sends the prophet Nathan to David; Nathan tells him a story about a rich man with many flocks who took a poor man's ONE little ewe lamb -- the lamb 'grew up together with him, and with his children; it did eat of his own meat, and drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was unto him as a daughter' -- and killed it for a traveler's dinner. David burns with anger and says the rich man deserves to die. Nathan answers: 'Thou art the man' (2 Samuel 12:1-7). T5: David says 'I have sinned against the LORD'; the baby dies; David fasts seven days on the ground, then rises, washes, and eats -- 'I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me' (12:23). Further rungs: David and Bathsheba's second son is Solomon (12:24); Psalm 51 is traditionally 'a Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came unto him' -- 'Have mercy upon me, O God... Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me' (Psalm 51:10); Uriah the Hittite's name appears in the list of David's mighty men at 2 Samuel 23:39.

name: Solomon: wisdom, the two mothers, the Temple, and the Queen of Sheba
scope: The son of David who asked for wisdom, split a baby to find its mother, built the great Temple, and stunned a foreign queen. T1: OPENING SCENE -- young King Solomon at the high place at Gibeon; God appears in a dream and says 'Ask what I shall give thee'; Solomon asks not for long life or riches but for 'an understanding heart to judge thy people' (1 Kings 3:5-9). T2: two harlots come to Solomon fighting over a living baby (the other's died in the night); Solomon calls for a sword and orders the child cut in two -- 'Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other' -- and the real mother cries 'give her the living child, and in no wise slay it', so Solomon knows and gives her the baby (1 Kings 3:16-28). T3: Solomon builds the Temple on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem in his fourth year (966 BC by traditional dating); its inner sanctuary, the Holy of Holies, is a windowless cube overlaid with pure gold, and inside stand two carved olive-wood cherubim ten cubits tall with wings touching wall to wall; the whole build takes seven years, and no hammer or axe is heard on the site -- the stones are cut at the quarry (1 Kings 6). T4: he sets up two great bronze pillars, JACHIN on the right and BOAZ on the left (1 Kings 7:21), and a huge round bronze basin, 'the molten sea', ten cubits across resting on twelve bronze oxen facing the four directions (1 Kings 7:23-26). T5: the Queen of Sheba arrives with camels of spices, gold, and precious stones to test him with hard questions; when she sees his court, his food, his cupbearers, and 'his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD', 'there was no more spirit in her' -- and she says 'the half was not told me' (1 Kings 10:1-7). Further rungs: Solomon writing three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs (1 Kings 4:32); the seven-branched menorah of pure hammered gold ordered back at Exodus 25:31-40 that stands in the Temple; the showbread (twelve loaves for the twelve tribes) on the golden table; the ark carried up on staves into the Holy of Holies; Solomon's 700 wives and 300 concubines and the foreign shrines that turn his heart in old age (1 Kings 11).

Geography bank may cover the Temple Mount as a PLACE -- theology owns what happened IN the Temple in story (the cherubim, the ark carried in, the cloud filling the house).

name: Elijah at Cherith and Zarephath (the ravens + the widow's oil)
scope: The prophet Elijah in hiding during the long drought he called down on King Ahab. T1: OPENING SCENE -- Elijah the Tishbite tells King Ahab of Israel and his Phoenician queen Jezebel that there will be no rain 'these years, but according to my word' (1 Kings 17:1); then God sends him to hide by the brook Cherith east of the Jordan. T2: RAVENS bring Elijah bread and flesh in the morning and bread and flesh in the evening, and he drinks from the brook -- until the brook dries up (17:4-7). T3: God sends him north to Zarephath, a town in Phoenician Sidon (Jezebel's own homeland); at the town gate a widow is gathering two sticks to bake a last little cake for herself and her son before they starve; Elijah asks her for water and a morsel of bread first (17:9-12). T4: she does, and the barrel of meal does not waste and the cruse of oil does not fail 'according to the word of the LORD' through the whole drought (17:14-16). T5: her son later falls sick and dies; Elijah carries him up to the loft where he is staying, lays him on his own bed, and stretches himself on the child three times crying to God; the child revives and Elijah brings him down: 'See, thy son liveth' (17:17-24). Further rungs: three and a half years of no rain (Luke 4:25 and James 5:17 give the length); Ahab's steward Obadiah hides 100 prophets fifty to a cave and feeds them bread and water while Jezebel is killing prophets (1 Kings 18:3-4); Elijah calling Ahab 'thou troubler of Israel' (18:17-18).

name: Mount Carmel: Elijah and the prophets of Baal
scope: The public duel that ended the drought, on the top of Mount Carmel above the sea. T1: OPENING SCENE -- Elijah gathers all Israel to Mount Carmel with 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of the grove (Asherah) that eat at Queen Jezebel's table (1 Kings 18:19-21). T2: 'How long halt ye between two opinions?' Elijah says; 'if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him.' The people answer him not a word. He proposes the contest: two bullocks on two altars, no fire, and 'the God that answereth by fire, let him be God' (18:21-24). T3: the prophets of Baal go first, from morning to noon, crying 'O Baal, hear us'; Elijah mocks them: 'Cry aloud: for he is a god; either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is in a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth, and must be awaked' (18:27); they cut themselves with knives and lancets 'till the blood gushed out upon them' -- and still no fire. T4: Elijah rebuilds a broken altar of twelve stones (one for each tribe of Israel), digs a trench around it, lays the wood and the bullock, and orders FOUR barrels of water poured over it THREE times -- twelve barrels -- till the trench runs full; then he prays a short prayer, and the fire of the LORD falls and consumes the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust, AND the water in the trench (18:30-38). T5: the people fall on their faces: 'The LORD, he is the God; the LORD, he is the God'; Elijah brings the prophets of Baal down to the brook Kishon and slays them there. Then he climbs Carmel, casts himself down with his face between his knees, and sends his servant seven times to look toward the sea; the seventh time the servant says there is 'a little cloud out of the sea, like a man's hand', and rain comes in a great deluge (18:41-45). Further rungs: Elijah tucks up his robe and outruns Ahab's chariot back to Jezreel (18:46).

name: Horeb: the still small voice + the fiery chariot
scope: Elijah broken after Carmel, and Elijah taken up. T1: OPENING SCENE -- Jezebel swears by her gods to have Elijah killed within the day; the greatest of the prophets, hours after the fire fell, RUNS for his life. He goes a day's journey into the wilderness, sits under a juniper tree, and asks to die: 'It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life' (1 Kings 19:4). T2: an angel wakes him twice with a cake baked on coals and a cruse of water; in the strength of that meat he walks forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God, and lodges in a cave (19:5-9). T3: God tells him to stand on the mount; a great and strong wind rends the mountains and breaks the rocks -- but the LORD is not in the wind. After the wind an earthquake -- but the LORD is not in the earthquake. After the earthquake a fire -- but the LORD is not in the fire. And after the fire 'a still small voice' (19:11-12). T4: Elijah wraps his face in his mantle at the cave's mouth; God tells him three things to do -- anoint Hazael king of Syria, anoint Jehu king of Israel, and anoint Elisha as prophet in his place -- and adds that seven thousand in Israel have not bowed the knee to Baal (19:15-18). T5: at the end of his days Elijah walks with Elisha across the Jordan (having struck the water with his rolled-up mantle so they cross dry-shod); a chariot of fire and horses of fire appear, and Elijah goes up by a WHIRLWIND into heaven -- and Elisha cries 'My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof!' (2 Kings 2:11-12). Further rungs: Elisha picks up the mantle that falls from him and asks a double portion of Elijah's spirit (2 Kings 2:9-14); Elijah returns in vision at the Transfiguration with Moses (Mark 9:4) -- a NT echo, name it as such if used.

name: Elisha: the double portion, the bears, and the axe head
scope: Elijah's successor in the mantle -- a working prophet whose miracles are stubbornly practical and sometimes disturbing. T1: OPENING SCENE -- Elisha son of Shaphat is plowing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah passes and throws his mantle on him; Elisha slaughters his oxen, uses the plow-wood to boil the meat, feeds the people, and follows Elijah (1 Kings 19:19-21). T2: at Elijah's departure Elisha asks for 'a double portion of thy spirit'; when Elijah is taken up in the whirlwind the mantle falls, and Elisha picks it up, strikes the Jordan, and says 'Where is the LORD God of Elijah?' -- and the waters part for him too (2 Kings 2:9-14). T3: at Bethel a gang of small boys mocks him, calling 'Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head'; Elisha turns and curses them in the name of the LORD, and TWO SHE-BEARS come out of the wood and tear forty-two of them (2 Kings 2:23-24). T4: a young prophet cutting timber by the Jordan drops a borrowed axe head into the water and cries out; Elisha cuts a stick, throws it in at the spot, and the iron floats to the surface (2 Kings 6:5-7). T5: Naaman the great Syrian general is a leper; a captive Israelite servant girl tells his wife of the prophet in Samaria; Naaman comes with silver and gold, and Elisha sends a servant out to tell him to wash SEVEN times in the Jordan; Naaman is furious ('Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel?') but his servants persuade him; he dips seven times and 'his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child' (2 Kings 5:1-14). Further rungs: the widow's pot of oil filling every borrowed vessel in the house (2 Kings 4:1-7); the Shunammite woman's little room on the wall with a bed, table, stool, and candlestick, and Elisha raising her son from the dead (2 Kings 4:8-37); the poisoned pot -- 'there is death in the pot' -- fixed with a handful of meal (4:38-41); Elisha's servant Gehazi getting Naaman's leprosy for chasing after the silver (2 Kings 5:20-27); Elisha's bones raising a dead man dropped hastily into his tomb by grave-robbers scared off by a Moabite raid (2 Kings 13:20-21).

SYMMETRIC-VOICE check: 'the man of God' is doctrinal shorthand -- use 'Elisha' or 'the prophet'. DISTRACTOR MINE = adjacent real prophet-miracles (Elijah's ravens vs Elisha's oil-pot; the man raised by Elijah at Zarephath vs the Shunammite's son raised by Elisha -- keep them straight; Aaron's rod that swallowed the magicians' rods; the manna and quail). DINNER-TEST payoff = the AXE HEAD floating (specific + kid-memorable) and the TWO she-bears (specific + hard). Accuracy rail: 2 Kings KJV verbatim; the bears are SHE-bears and there are TWO; forty-two children; Naaman dips SEVEN times.
history_overlap: History bank may cover 9th-century Aram-Damascus and the House of Omri; theology owns the STORY beats -- the mantle from the whirlwind, the two she-bears, the floating axe head, the seven dips of Naaman.

name: Daniel in the lions' den
scope: The Judean exile who prayed at his open window and spent a night sealed in a pit of lions. T1: OPENING SCENE -- Daniel is now old, serving under Darius the Mede, and the king plans to set him over the whole realm; the other satraps hate him and plot to trap him with a decree that for thirty days no one may ask a petition of any god or man except the king, on pain of the lions' den (Daniel 6:1-9). T2: Daniel goes home, opens his upper windows toward Jerusalem, and kneels down three times a day to pray and give thanks 'as he did aforetime' -- exactly what he had always done (6:10). T3: caught, and dragged before the king, Daniel is thrown into the den; a great stone is laid on the mouth of the pit and sealed with the king's own signet and his lords' signets so no one can change it (6:16-17). T4: the king spends the night fasting, refuses music, and cannot sleep; at first light he runs to the pit and cries with a lamentable voice: 'O Daniel, servant of the living God, is thy God, whom thou servest continually, able to deliver thee from the lions?' Daniel answers: 'My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me' (6:19-22). T5: the king brings Daniel up 'no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he believed in his God'; the accusers, their wives, and their children are thrown to the lions instead and the lions break all their bones before they hit the bottom (6:23-24). Further rungs: Daniel earlier at the Babylonian court refusing the king's meat and wine and thriving on pulse and water (Daniel 1); 'Belteshazzar' as the Babylonian name given him (1:7); the specific detail that Daniel prays THREE times a day toward JERUSALEM at open windows (6:10) -- the reason he could be trapped is that his habit was fixed and visible.

DISTRACTOR MINE = other real OT captivity + court scenes (Joseph in Pharaoh's court; Nehemiah before Artaxerxes; Esther before Xerxes; the three friends in the furnace); other real miracle-of-shut-mouths scenes. DINNER-TEST payoff = the WINDOWS TOWARD JERUSALEM three times a day (his prayer habit was fixed and public -- that is why he was trapped) and the accusers' children thrown in after. name: Belshazzar's feast and the writing on the wall
scope: A drunk Babylonian king, the stolen Temple vessels, and a hand appearing to write on the wall. T1: OPENING SCENE -- King Belshazzar throws a great feast for a thousand of his lords and orders the gold and silver VESSELS his father Nebuchadnezzar carried off from the Temple in Jerusalem brought in, so the king, his lords, his wives, and his concubines can drink wine out of them (Daniel 5:1-4). T2: as they drink they praise 'the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone.' In the same hour the fingers of a MAN'S HAND come out and write on the plaster of the wall opposite the great candlestick, and the king watches the hand that writes (5:5). T3: the king's face changes, the joints of his loins are loosed, his knees smite one against another; his astrologers and Chaldeans cannot read the writing. The queen (the queen-mother) remembers the Judean captive Daniel from Nebuchadnezzar's days and calls him in; Belshazzar promises a scarlet robe, a gold chain, and to make him third ruler in the kingdom (5:6-16). T4: Daniel refuses the gifts and reads the four words: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN -- 'MENE: God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it. TEKEL: Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting. PERES: Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians' (5:25-28). T5: 'in that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain', and Darius the Median takes the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old (5:30-31). Further rungs: the golden candlestick and Temple vessels stolen by Nebuchadnezzar at 2 Kings 25:14-15; the reason the writing appears is specifically the desecration of the Temple cups; the fact that Belshazzar's father is 'Nebuchadnezzar' in the story though historically he was son of Nabonidus (label as a story-vs-archaeology point at T5).

DISTRACTOR MINE = other real OT judgment-oracles (Jonah's 'Yet forty days'; Isaiah's oracles against Babylon; Nebuchadnezzar's tree-dream at Daniel 4). DINNER-TEST payoff = the four Aramaic words and 'weighed in the balances, and art found wanting' -- one of the phrases everyone quotes without knowing where it's from. Accuracy rail: Daniel 5 KJV verbatim; the four words MENE MENE TEKEL UPHARSIN are one of the very few Aramaic phrases preserved -- keep them exact.

name: Nebuchadnezzar's dream and the fiery furnace (Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego)
scope: The dream of the great image and the three friends in the burning furnace. T1: OPENING SCENE -- King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon has a dream that troubles him but will not remember it; he decrees all his wise men be killed if they cannot BOTH tell him the dream AND its meaning; Daniel asks for time, prays, and comes back with both (Daniel 2:1-19). T2: the dream is a great image -- head of fine GOLD, breast and arms of SILVER, belly and thighs of BRASS, legs of IRON, feet part of iron and part of CLAY. A stone 'cut out without hands' strikes the feet and the whole image breaks into pieces, and the stone becomes a great mountain that fills the earth (2:31-35, 44-45). T3: later Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image sixty cubits high in the plain of Dura and orders that when the horn, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of music sound, everyone must fall down and worship it (Daniel 3:1-5). T4: three young Judeans -- Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (the Babylonian names of Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah) -- refuse; brought before the king, they say: 'If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up' (3:17-18). T5: the furnace is heated SEVEN TIMES hotter than usual; the flame kills the strong men who throw them in; the three walk in the fire unbound, and Nebuchadnezzar rises in astonishment: 'Lo, I see FOUR men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God' (3:24-25). They come out with not a hair singed, not a coat scorched, not even the smell of fire on them (3:27). Further rungs: Nebuchadnezzar later going mad and eating grass like an ox with hair like eagles' feathers and nails like birds' claws (Daniel 4:33) after boasting on his palace roof -- the tree-vision dream Daniel had already told him.

DINNER-TEST payoff = the FOURTH figure in the fire and 'but if not' (the three young men's refusal that stands even if no rescue comes). name: Jonah: the great fish, Nineveh, and the gourd vine
scope: The prophet who ran from a job and got swallowed on the way. T1: OPENING SCENE -- God tells Jonah son of Amittai to go to Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, and preach against it; Jonah instead pays his fare and boards a ship at Joppa going the OPPOSITE way, to Tarshish (Jonah 1:1-3). T2: a great storm comes; the sailors cast lots to find the guilty man and the lot falls on Jonah, asleep in the ship's hold; he tells them to throw him overboard, they row hard but can't, and finally do; the sea is calm at once (1:4-15). T3: 'the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah', and he is in its belly THREE days and three nights; from inside he prays -- 'I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD... out of the belly of hell cried I' -- and the fish vomits him onto dry land (Jonah 1:17 - 2:10). T4: Nineveh is 'an exceeding great city of three days' journey'; Jonah walks in a day's journey and cries: 'Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!' The people, from the greatest to the least, put on sackcloth; the king rises from his throne, puts on sackcloth and sits in ashes, and even decrees that beast, herd, and flock be covered with sackcloth and given no food or water. God relents (3:1-10). T5: Jonah is furious -- he says he KNEW God would relent, that's why he ran! He sits east of the city under a booth to wait and see. God prepares a GOURD (a fast-growing vine) to shade his head, and Jonah is 'exceeding glad of the gourd'; but at dawn God prepares a WORM that smites the gourd so it withers, then a hot east wind and sun so Jonah faints and again asks to die. God answers: 'Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for which thou hast not laboured... and should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also much cattle?' (Jonah 4). Further rungs: Nineveh's fall in 612 BC to the Medes and Babylonians as history-bank material (name at T5 if used); Jesus later refers to 'the sign of the prophet Jonah' at Matthew 12:39-40 (NT echo, only if the rung is EXPLICITLY the echo).

framing_note: ANTI-RESTATEMENT rail: put the pointed detail in the stem (Joppa, Tarshish, asleep in the hold, three days and three nights, 'Yet forty days', beasts in sackcloth, the WORM at dawn) and ask the named thing (Jonah; Nineveh; the gourd; 'more than sixscore thousand that cannot discern between their right hand and their left'). SYMMETRIC-VOICE check: tell it flat; the book itself is COMIC and self-critical, tell it that way (Jonah runs, is furious that mercy worked, mourns a plant). DISTRACTOR MINE = other real OT storm-and-fish beats (Noah's flood; Peter walking on the sea -- NT, wrong; the storm on Galilee); other real repentant cities. DINNER-TEST payoff = beasts in sackcloth (kids will remember this) and the WORM that eats the shade plant at dawn. Accuracy rail: Jonah 1-4 KJV verbatim; the text says 'great fish' not 'whale' -- do NOT let a stem say 'whale' (that's the popular tradition, not the KJV).
history_overlap: History bank owns Assyrian archaeology and the actual Nineveh (Sennacherib's palace + the Library of Ashurbanipal, fall 612 BC); geography owns Nineveh as a PLACE across the Tigris from modern Mosul; theology owns the STORY -- the fish, the sackcloth on beasts, the gourd and the worm.

name: Esther, Mordecai, Haman, and the feast of Purim
scope: A Jewish orphan becomes queen of Persia and stops a genocide. T1: OPENING SCENE -- King Ahasuerus (Xerxes) holds a 180-day feast at Shushan (Susa) the palace; when Queen Vashti refuses to be paraded before the drunken lords, she is deposed; a beauty search brings the young Jewish orphan Hadassah, raised by her cousin Mordecai, and she is crowned queen under the name Esther; Mordecai tells her not to reveal she is a Jew (Esther 1-2). T2: Haman the Agagite, the king's favorite, is furious that Mordecai will not bow to him at the gate; he casts PUR (the LOT) to pick a day and buys an edict for ten thousand talents of silver to destroy all the Jews in the empire on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar (3:1-13). T3: Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and sends word to Esther: 'For if thou altogether holdest thy peace at this time... who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?' Esther fasts three days and says: 'if I perish, I perish' (4:14-16). T4: Esther comes uninvited into the king's inner court (a death penalty unless he holds out the golden sceptre); he does. She invites the king and Haman to a banquet, and then to a second. That night the king cannot sleep, reads in the chronicles, and finds Mordecai had once saved his life from the assassins Bigthan and Teresh and had never been rewarded; when Haman arrives at dawn asking to hang Mordecai on a fifty-cubit gallows he has built in his own courtyard, the king instead makes Haman parade Mordecai through the city on the royal horse in the royal robes crying 'Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour' (6:1-11). T5: at the second banquet Esther names Haman as the enemy; the king in fury steps out into the garden; Haman falls on Esther's couch begging; the king returns and takes it for assault. A eunuch mentions Haman's own gallows -- 'Hang him thereon' (7:9-10). The Jews defend themselves on the appointed day, and the days of PURIM (from PUR, the lot) become an annual feast of joy, gift-giving, and rescue (9:20-28). Further rungs: the book of Esther is the ONE book in the Hebrew Bible that never uses the name of God; Haman's ten sons hanged (9:14); the extravagant length of Haman's fifty-cubit gallows (~75 ft) built the night before.

DISTRACTOR MINE = other real Persian court figures (Cyrus, Darius, Artaxerxes, Nehemiah's Sanballat + Tobiah; Daniel's Darius the Mede); other real feast-names (Passover, Hanukkah, Sukkot, Yom Kippur -- distinguish Purim clearly). DINNER-TEST payoff = Haman hanged on his OWN gallows and 'for such a time as this'. Accuracy rail: Esther KJV verbatim; the king is Ahasuerus in the text (traditionally identified with Xerxes I). The 'God never named' point is a real textual fact worth a T5 rung.

name: Ezekiel: the wheel and the valley of dry bones
scope: The exile priest by the river Chebar who sees the strangest vision in the Bible and preaches to a valley of bones. T1: OPENING SCENE -- Ezekiel the priest is a captive in Babylon by the river Chebar in his thirtieth year when the heavens open and he sees a great cloud coming out of the north with fire enfolding itself and a brightness around it (Ezekiel 1:1-4). T2: out of the fire come FOUR living creatures, each with FOUR faces -- a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle -- and each with four wings; their feet are like a calf's, and they sparkle like burnished brass (1:5-14). T3: beside each creature is a WHEEL 'as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel', the rims are 'so high that they were dreadful', and 'they were full of eyes round about'; wherever the creatures go, the wheels go -- and above them a firmament like crystal, and above the firmament a throne of sapphire, and on the throne 'the appearance of a man' surrounded by a rainbow (Ezekiel 1:15-28). T4: God sets Ezekiel down in the midst of a VALLEY full of very many, very DRY bones and asks: 'Son of man, can these bones live?' Ezekiel answers 'O Lord God, thou knowest' (Ezekiel 37:1-3). T5: Ezekiel prophesies as he is told; there is a NOISE, a SHAKING, and the bones come together, bone to his bone; sinews, then flesh, then skin cover them -- but no breath in them. Then he prophesies to the four winds, breath comes into them, they stand up on their feet 'an exceeding great army' (37:7-10). Further rungs: Ezekiel eating the scroll that tastes sweet as honey (Ezekiel 3:1-3); lying on his left side 390 days and his right side 40 days as a sign against Jerusalem (Ezekiel 4:4-6); Ezekiel forbidden to mourn when his wife dies suddenly, as a sign to the people (Ezekiel 24:15-18).

name: Isaiah: coals to the lips and the seraphim
scope: The Jerusalem prophet's call-vision in the Temple. T1: OPENING SCENE -- 'In the year that king Uzziah died' Isaiah sees God sitting on a throne 'high and lifted up', and his train (the hem of his robe) fills the Temple (Isaiah 6:1). T2: above the throne stand the SERAPHIM, each with SIX WINGS -- 'with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly' -- and they cry to one another: 'Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory' (6:2-3). T3: the doorposts shake at the voice and the house fills with smoke; Isaiah cries 'Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips' (6:4-5). T4: one of the seraphim flies to him with a LIVE COAL taken with tongs from the altar and touches it to his mouth: 'Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged' (6:6-7). T5: God asks 'Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?' Isaiah answers 'Here am I; send me' (6:8). Further rungs: Isaiah walking barefoot and naked for three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia (Isaiah 20:2-4); Isaiah delivering the message to King Ahaz about a virgin conceiving and calling him Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14); Isaiah promising King Hezekiah, sick unto death, that the sun's shadow will go BACKWARD ten degrees on the sundial of Ahaz as the sign of his healing (2 Kings 20:8-11 / Isaiah 38:7-8).

name: Jeremiah: the potter's wheel and the linen loincloth
scope: The reluctant weeping prophet and his teaching signs, on the eve of Jerusalem's fall. T1: OPENING SCENE -- God's word comes to young Jeremiah in the days of King Josiah; Jeremiah objects: 'Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child.' God tells him not to say that and touches his mouth: 'Behold, I have put my words in thy mouth' (Jeremiah 1:6-9). T2: God tells Jeremiah to go DOWN to the potter's house; the potter is working at his WHEELS, and the vessel he is making is marred in his hand, so he makes it again into another vessel 'as seemed good to the potter to make it'; God says 'as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel' (Jeremiah 18:1-6). T3: God tells Jeremiah to buy a LINEN LOINCLOTH (a girdle), wear it without washing, then go to the Euphrates and hide it in the cleft of a rock; many days later he digs it up and it is MARRED, profitable for nothing -- a sign that God will spoil the pride of Judah in exactly that way (Jeremiah 13:1-11). T4: Jeremiah stands in the Temple gate and preaches; the priest Pashur beats him and puts him in the STOCKS overnight (Jeremiah 20:1-2); later Jeremiah is thrown into a MIRY DUNGEON, a cistern, and sinks in the mire; an Ethiopian eunuch named Ebed-melech pulls him up with old rags and rotten rags let down with cords under his armpits (Jeremiah 38:6-13). T5: as the Babylonians besiege Jerusalem, Jeremiah buys his cousin Hanamel's field at Anathoth for seventeen shekels of silver, signs and seals the deed, and puts it in an earthen vessel to preserve it 'many days' -- a sign that houses and fields shall again be bought in this land (Jeremiah 32:6-15). Further rungs: 'the leopard cannot change his spots' (Jeremiah 13:23); the burning of Jeremiah's scroll by King Jehoiakim, who cut it with the penknife and threw it into the hearth-fire piece by piece, and Jeremiah dictated it again (Jeremiah 36:20-32); Jeremiah's 'is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by?' in Lamentations 1:12.

name: Solomon's Temple: menorah, showbread, and the two cherubim
scope: The specific SACRED OBJECTS in the great Temple at Jerusalem, all named. T1: OPENING SCENE -- inside the Holy Place stands a MENORAH, a seven-branched lampstand of pure hammered gold (a talent of pure gold), with almond-blossom cups, knops, and flowers running down each of its six branches and the central shaft -- ordered in detail at Exodus 25:31-40 and standing in the Temple. T2: on the golden table opposite the menorah rests the SHOWBREAD -- twelve loaves in two rows of six, one loaf for each of the twelve tribes of Israel, replaced every sabbath, and eaten only by the priests (Exodus 25:23-30; Leviticus 24:5-9). T3: beyond the veil, in the windowless Holy of Holies, stand two carved olive-wood CHERUBIM ten cubits tall (about 15 feet), overlaid with pure gold, their wings each five cubits so that wing tip touches wing tip stretched across the entire chamber (1 Kings 6:23-28). T4: the ARK of the Covenant is carried in on staves and placed BENEATH those wings, its own two golden cherubim facing each other on its lid, the mercy seat; inside the ark, the tables of stone Moses laid there at Horeb (1 Kings 8:6-9). T5: at the dedication a cloud fills the house so the priests cannot stand to minister, 'for the glory of the LORD had filled the house of the LORD'; Solomon says 'I have surely built thee an house to dwell in, a settled place for thee to abide in for ever' (1 Kings 8:10-13). Further rungs: the altar of incense of gold before the veil (1 Kings 7:48); the bronze altar of burnt offering in the courtyard; the ten smaller lampstands (five on each side) added by Solomon (1 Kings 7:49); the destruction of the Temple by Nebuchadnezzar's captain Nebuzaradan on the seventh day of the fifth month, 586 BC, and the loss of the ark thereafter (2 Kings 25).

framing_note: This is the OBJECTS ladder -- named artifacts of the Temple. ANTI-RESTATEMENT rail: put the pointed detail in the stem (SEVEN branches with almond-blossom knops; TWELVE loaves in two rows of six; TWO olive-wood cherubim TEN cubits tall with wings touching wall to wall) and ask for the named object (menorah; showbread; the cherubim; the ark; the mercy seat). SYMMETRIC-VOICE check: name objects like Mjolnir + Gungnir + Draupnir in the Norse ladder or Excalibur + Round Table + Grail in the Arthurian -- these are the great sacred objects of ONE tradition, told in the same register. DISTRACTOR MINE = other real OT sacred objects (Aaron's rod that budded; the golden pot of manna; the tables of stone; the brazen serpent Nehushtan; the ephod; the Urim and Thummim). DINNER-TEST payoff = TWELVE loaves of showbread (one for each tribe, changed every sabbath, eaten only by priests) and the two carved olive-wood cherubim so large their wingtips touched wall to wall. name: Elijah's mantle and the harp of David: the objects that name their bearers
scope: The signature named objects carried by kings and prophets in this strand. T1: OPENING SCENE -- young David is called to King Saul's court because Saul is tormented; David plays on his HARP (a lyre) and 'Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him' (1 Samuel 16:23). T2: Saul, one day, hurls his SPEAR at David as he plays, twice, and David slips away (1 Samuel 18:10-11; 19:9-10) -- David's harp and Saul's spear are their signature objects. T3: Elijah's MANTLE (his prophet's cloak of hair) is thrown across young Elisha at the plow (1 Kings 19:19); at the Jordan Elijah wraps it up and strikes the water and the river parts; taken up in the whirlwind, the mantle falls, and Elisha picks it up and repeats the strike -- the mantle is the sign of the succession (2 Kings 2:8-14). T4: John the Baptist much later wears 'raiment of camel's hair, and a leathern girdle about his loins' (Matthew 3:4), echoing Elijah's own leathern girdle (2 Kings 1:8) -- so the mantle is a shape that carries across centuries in the story (name at T5 depth as a THEME rung). T5: Solomon's TWO PILLARS in front of the Temple porch have their own proper names, JACHIN ('he shall establish') on the right and BOAZ ('in him is strength') on the left (1 Kings 7:21); they are landmarks whose names are still spoken. Further rungs: David's SLING and shepherd's BAG (1 Samuel 17:40); Saul's crown and bracelet stripped from his body (2 Samuel 1:10); the ROD that budded (Aaron's, Numbers 17); the JAWBONE of an ass that Samson uses (Judges 15:15).

framing_note: This ladder is deliberately the NAMED OBJECTS one -- meets the answer-hierarchy rule (named things are best). ANTI-RESTATEMENT rail: put the pointed detail in the stem (calmed Saul when the evil spirit came; struck the Jordan and it parted; JACHIN on the right; BOAZ on the left) and ask for the named object or figure (harp; mantle; the two pillar names). DISTRACTOR MINE = other real named OT objects (Aaron's rod, the brazen serpent Nehushtan, the golden pot of manna, the tables of stone, the ephod, Urim and Thummim, Samson's jawbone of an ass); wrong named objects from adjacent traditions (Excalibur, Mjolnir -- pillar-name distractors could include real other pillar names). name: 'Choose you this day whom ye shall serve': Joshua at Shechem
scope: The old warrior Joshua's farewell speech, one of the most-quoted lines in the OT. T1: OPENING SCENE -- Joshua, now 'stricken in age' at 110, gathers all the tribes of Israel at SHECHEM at the end of his life, calling for their elders, their heads, their judges, and their officers to stand before God (Joshua 24:1). T2: he retells the whole story from Abraham through Egypt through the wilderness to the settled land ('I sent hornets before you, which drave them out from before you'), then puts the challenge: 'Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth: and put away the gods which your fathers served on the other side of the flood, and in Egypt' (24:14). T3: the pointed line: 'And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye shall serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' (24:15). T4: he sets up a GREAT STONE under the oak that is by the sanctuary of the LORD at Shechem: 'Behold, this stone shall be a witness unto us; for it hath heard all the words of the LORD which he spake unto us: it shall be therefore a witness unto you, lest ye deny your God' (24:26-27). T5: Joshua dies at 110 and is buried in his own inheritance at Timnath-serah in Mount Ephraim; the bones of Joseph, carried up out of Egypt, are buried at Shechem in a parcel of ground Jacob bought for a hundred pieces of silver (24:29-33). Further rungs: Joshua earlier at Jericho circling the walls seven days with seven priests blowing seven ram's-horn trumpets, and on the seventh day going round seven times, and the walls falling down flat (Joshua 6); the sun standing still on Gibeon and the moon in the valley of Ajalon 'about a whole day' (Joshua 10:12-13).

ANTI-RESTATEMENT rail: put the pointed detail in the stem (SHECHEM as the place; the great stone set up under the oak as a WITNESS; walking around Jericho seven days with seven priests and rams' horns) and ask the named thing (Joshua; 'choose you this day whom ye shall serve'; the sun on Gibeon). SYMMETRIC-VOICE check: tell it in plain narrative; the choice-speech is Joshua speaking, not the bank endorsing. DISTRACTOR MINE = other real OT prophet-and-king assemblies (Samuel at Mizpah; Solomon at Gibeon; the Rehoboam/Jeroboam split at Shechem later); other real farewell speeches (Moses at Nebo). DINNER-TEST payoff = 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD' -- almost everyone can finish the sentence, few know Joshua said it at Shechem.
